units.name: http-api
units.role: Orchestrate the request lifecycle and expose the functions/Session object users call.
units.description: This is the part of the library that ordinary users touch directly: the requests.get/post/put/patch/delete/head/options functions and the Session object. Given a method, a URL, and options like headers, auth, or cookies, it builds the request, sends it, follows any redirects the server asks for, and keeps track of cookies and settings across multiple calls made through the same session. It does not itself understand HTTP wire format or open sockets — it delegates those jobs to other parts of the library and focuses purely on orchestrating the overall request lifecycle.

units.name: request-response-model
units.role: Define what an HTTP request and response are: build the wire-ready request, expose the response.
units.description: This code defines the two core ideas of the whole library: an HTTP 'request' and an HTTP 'response'. It takes a simple, high-level description of what someone wants to send (a URL, headers, form data, files, JSON, cookies) and turns it into a fully-formed, wire-ready request with a correct URL, headers, and body. It also defines what a 'response' looks like once one comes back: the status code, headers, cookies, redirect history, and convenient ways to read the body as raw bytes, text, or parsed JSON. This is the shared vocabulary the rest of the library uses to talk about requests and responses; it never opens a network connection itself.

units.name: connection-adapter
units.role: Move a prepared request to and from a real server over urllib3 connection pools.
units.description: This is the part of the library that actually opens a network connection to a server and talks HTTP over it. It takes a fully-prepared outgoing request, hands it to the underlying networking engine (urllib3) to open a TCP connection (with TLS certificate checking and optional proxying), sends the request over the wire, and converts whatever comes back into this library's own Response object. It also manages a pool of reusable connections so repeated requests to the same server don't have to reconnect every time, and cleans those connections up when asked.

units.name: auth-schemes
units.role: Attach the right credentials (Basic/Proxy/Digest) to an outgoing request.
units.description: This unit defines the different ways a caller can prove its identity to a web server: sending a plain username and password (HTTP Basic Auth), doing the same for a proxy server (Proxy Auth), or performing the more secure Digest Auth handshake where the server issues a one-time challenge on a 401 response and the client computes a cryptographic reply to it. Given an outgoing request, it attaches the right 'Authorization' or 'Proxy-Authorization' header, and for Digest Auth it arranges to automatically retry the request once the server's challenge has been received.

units.name: cookie-jar
units.role: Adapt Request/Response objects to Python's stdlib cookie-jar machinery.
units.description: This unit is the bridge between how the library represents HTTP cookies and Python's built-in cookie-jar machinery. It knows how to read 'Set-Cookie' headers from a server response and remember them, and how to figure out which stored cookies should be sent back on a later request to the same site. It also provides a friendlier, dictionary-like way to inspect and edit cookies without needing to understand the more awkward standard-library interface underneath. It only manages the small blobs of state (cookies) that travel alongside requests and responses; it does not decide what a request or response is.

units.name: http-support-utils
units.role: Supporting operations for talking to the environment and normalizing wire data.
units.description: This is a toolbox of helper functions the library uses to deal with its surrounding computer environment: figuring out whether to use a proxy server and where to find its settings, reading saved login credentials from a netrc file, writing files safely to disk, guessing the character encoding or filename of data, and validating or requoting pieces of a web address or HTTP header. It doesn't decide what a 'request' or 'response' is — it provides the practical, low-level plumbing that the rest of the library relies on, and it's written so people using the library directly can reuse the same helpers in their own code.

units.name: status-codes

units.description: This is a phrasebook that translates the numeric codes web servers use to describe what happened with a request (like 404 for 'not found' or 200 for 'okay') into easy-to-remember names. Other parts of the program use these friendly names, for example to check 'is this a redirect', instead of hard-coding the raw numbers themselves.

units.name: collections
units.role: Generic dict-like containers used throughout the library.
units.description: This provides two simple, general-purpose containers used everywhere else in the library: a dictionary that treats string keys as case-insensitive (so 'Content-Type' and 'content-type' are the same entry), used for storing HTTP headers, and a dictionary whose values can also be looked up as attributes, used for the human-readable names of HTTP status codes. Neither structure knows anything about HTTP itself; they are reusable building blocks that other parts of the library plug into.

units.name: exceptions
units.role: The catalog of everything that can go wrong when making a request.
units.description: This is the catalog of everything that can go wrong when the library makes an HTTP request: connection failures, timeouts, bad or missing URLs, too many redirects, invalid headers, malformed JSON responses, and so on, plus a couple of warning classes for deprecated usage. It does not perform any actions itself; it defines named error and warning types, arranged in a small inheritance hierarchy (e.g. ConnectTimeout is both a ConnectionError and a Timeout), that the rest of the library raises and that calling code can catch to react appropriately.

units.name: diagnostics
units.role: Report the installed environment for bug reports.
units.description: This is a small, self-contained debugging tool bundled with the library. When someone runs `python -m requests.help`, it collects information about the computer's software environment: the Python version, the operating system, the TLS library in use, and the version numbers of the library and its key dependencies, then prints it as neatly formatted JSON. Its purpose is to give bug reporters an easy way to paste their environment details when filing an issue.

units.name: foundation
units.role: Cross-cutting compatibility shims, version metadata, and package bootstrap.
units.description: This is the plumbing that everything else in the library is built on top of, but it does not itself know anything about making HTTP requests. It records the library's own version number, tells the rest of the code where to find the bundle of trusted security certificates, smooths over small differences between Python environments and optional third-party libraries (such as which JSON parser or character-detection library is installed), provides a handful of tiny reusable helper functions (like converting strings between text and byte types, or checking whether a request object is fully filled in), keeps old import paths like requests.packages.urllib3 working for backward compatibility, and performs one-time startup checks (verifying installed dependency versions are compatible, silencing noisy warnings, enabling extra TLS support if needed) when the package is first imported. It also re-exports the names other units define (get, post, Session, codes, the exception classes, ...) as the package's public surface.

effects.description: Resolves the on-disk path to the bundled CA certificate bundle via certifi.where() (certs.py); the file itself is opened later by connection-adapter.
Monkeypatches urllib3/pyopenssl to add SNI support when the stdlib ssl module lacks it, and configures global logging/warnings filters, at package import time (__init__.py).
Mutates sys.modules at import time to alias urllib3/idna/chardet submodules under requests.packages.* for backward-compatible import paths (packages.py).

compat.py genuinely imports from the stdlib urllib.request module (getproxies, proxy_bypass, ...) for reading system/proxy configuration; it does not itself open connections. Also, __init__.py's module docstring contains a '>>> import requests' usage example, which a naive text-based effect scan flags as a network effect.

violations_observed.note: PreparedRequest.copy() calls cookies._copy_cookie_jar, a function named with a leading underscore (Python's private-by-convention marker), rather than going through cookie-jar's public surface (RequestsCookieJar, cookiejar_from_dict, get_cookie_header, extract_cookies_to_jar, merge_cookies). The source itself flags this with a `# cross-module usage in models.py` comment acknowledging the reach across the boundary. Recorded, not fixed.
